h1: Canned gin and tonic as a product line
title: Canned Gin and Tonic as a Product Line | Craft Beer School
desc: What it takes to add a canned gin and tonic to a gin brand: recipe, carbonation, can supply, regulation, shelf life and the economics against bottled gin.
teaser: A canned gin and tonic is a different business from a bottle of gin. It is a drinks manufacturer's problem as much as a distiller's.
standfirst: Ready-to-drink cans promise convenience and a new occasion. They also bring carbonation, packaging and regulation that a gin distillery may not yet handle.
sections:
A canned gin and tonic is a ready-to-drink product, an RTD. It combines gin, tonic water and sometimes sweetener, acid or flavour, carbonates the mix and seals it in a can. The strength is much lower than bottled gin because the spirit is diluted.

That makes it a beverage-manufacturing job. You need to control carbonation, dissolved oxygen, sugar or sweetener, acidity and microbial stability. A distillery has skills in the first step, which is the gin. The rest is closer to soft drinks and beer packaging.

Cans sell where a bottle does not: picnics, travel, events and places where glass is banned. They suit drinkers who want a measured, ready serve. They also open a separate price and margin structure.

They compete with other RTDs and with beer. Do your homework on shelf prices and occasions before you invest. Use the method in market research before launching a gin with RTD products in mind.
Making the recipe work in a can

A good home gin and tonic does not automatically make a good can. Check:

  • Balance: gin character must survive dilution and chilling.
  • Bitterness: tonic brings quinine bitterness, which must be balanced.
  • Carbonation: set the level carefully, because too little tastes flat and too much foams on filling.
  • Acid and sweetness: they affect taste and stability.
  • Oxygen: pick-up during filling and storage dulls aroma and citrus.

Run bench trials and then pilot-scale trials, tasting responsibly and in small measures. Store sample cans warm and cold. Check them weeks later.
Cans, filling and who does the work

Most small brands use a contract canner. Ask about minimum runs, can sizes, printing options, lead times and quality checks. Printed cans often need large minimum orders, so plain cans with a label or sleeve may suit a trial.

Filling a carbonated alcoholic drink needs the right equipment and a clean, controlled process. Doing it yourself is a large investment. A contract route spreads the risk, as discussed in contract-distilled gin. The same questions on ownership, specifications and release apply.

An RTD with spirit may be treated differently from the gin it contains. The licence class, the duty or tax rate, the label rules and where it can be sold can all differ. In India, alcohol is a state subject, so the treatment of RTDs varies by state. Check with the regulator or a licensing adviser before you commit to a recipe or a can print. Rules change.

Build a separate cost sheet. Include the gin used per can, the tonic and other ingredients, the can and ends, the label or print, filling, packaging into trays or cartons, freight and tax. Cold-chain or chilled display may add cost.

Compare the margin per can and the volume you need with your bottled gin. Cans may sell in larger numbers at a lower price per unit, so check the maths with your own figures. A canned line should add profit, not just activity.
Shelf life and the first order

A canned product is expected to last for months. Spirit gives it some stability, but sugar, acid, juice and carbonation all affect how it ages. Light and heat change citrus flavours. Hot storage and transport in a warm country speed that along.

Decide the shelf life you will print and test it. Store cans at room temperature, warm and chilled. Taste them against fresh ones over several months. Set a best-before date you can defend. In hot weather, cans left on a loading bay will not behave like cans in a cool lab.

Cans are bought in large lots and printed cans are bought in even larger ones. A first order of cans can be bigger than the first filling run, which ties up cash. Ask your canner for minimums in writing. Build the cash flow, the way you did for glass in gin packaging costs, before you place an order.

State strength, volume and ingredients as the rules require. Do not suggest that a ready-to-drink is a lighter or healthier choice. Do not target minors with imagery or flavours. A can that looks like a soft drink invites scrutiny.
faqs: Is a canned gin and tonic easy to add?
Not usually. It needs carbonation control, a can supply chain and often a different licence class.
Most small brands start with a contract canner. Own filling needs heavy investment.
Does the gin taste the same in a can?
Not automatically. Dilution, chilling and carbonation change it, so test the recipe in cans.
Not necessarily. Rules differ by country and Indian state. Check before you plan the price.
